_comment: Expected column sequences per case per format, derived from the five
settled contract rules — NOT recorded from whatever a runtime happened
to emit. Each entry is the EXACT ordered sequence of column names as they
must appear in that runtime's serialized output.
'sequence' is an ordered array and is compared element-by-element. It is
never treated as a set and never sorted: an assertion that ignored order
would be inert against exactly the bugs this suite exists to catch.
'empty': true means the formatter must emit no data row and no header row
(contract rule 4). For json/yaml an empty document (`[]`) satisfies it.
Runtimes listed under known_gaps deviate KNOWINGLY. Their divergence is
reported by the harness but does not fail it — see README.
Contract rule 3: header == key universally. The enforcement MECHANISM
differs per runtime (assert / dataclass __post_init__ / constructor
throw / read-time guard), so the fixture asserts the CONSTRAINT — a
header != key ColumnSpec must not round-trip — rather than pinning a
particular exception type or call site.
Go is absent by construction, not by oversight: a `table:""` tag cannot
express a header/key split at all. Go's inability to express it is the
REASON the rule exists, so Go satisfies it vacuously and the payload
SDKs are the ones under test.
Recorded divergences. The harness SURFACES these and does not fail on
them. Each is a real behavioral difference with a decided disposition.

detail: Go SELECTS the requested columns but never REORDERS them: it emits
them in struct-field declaration order regardless of the --cols
sequence. filterColumns (go/console/output/projection.go:13-17) builds
a `want` set and its own doc states 'Order is preserved from cols
(struct field order), not from selected'. structToMap (:111) does the
same for json/yaml.
This contradicts contract rule 2, which settled 4-to-1 with Go the
sole outlier and explicitly noted 'Only Go changes'. The Go-side
change was scoped to phase 2 but landed in none of T-0961..T-0965,
all four of which are payload SDKs. So this gap is the unimplemented
half of rule 2, not a new discovery — recorded here so it cannot
drift back out of view.
projectToMaps/structToMap (go/console/output/projection.go:52,:111)
build a map[string]any, so encoding/json and yaml.v3 emit keys
alphabetically. Go's rule-1/rule-2 ordering guarantee is therefore
table/csv/text-only. Go additionally switches key NAMES from the
json:/yaml: tags to the table: tag headers the moment cols is
non-empty.
Neither SDK registers a csv or text formatter — rs builtins.rs and
php Builtins.php both say csv/text land in a follow-up phase. The
extended cases therefore run on py/ts/go only. Reported as skipped,
never as passed.
priority is a complete hide-on-overflow feature in Go
(renderer.go:301-322 parseTableTag, :327-349 selectVisibleColumns,
:351-364 lowestPriorityIndex). The payload SDKs accept, store and
ignore it (contract rule 5). No conformance fixture asserts it:
pinning Go's behavior would pin a capability four runtimes cannot
mirror. Revisit when the port track lands.
Note Go's hiding is width-driven and terminalWidth() falls back to
200 columns for a non-TTY writer, so priority does not perturb these
fixtures.
py kept an optional 5th `columns` parameter on Formatter.render with
signature-gating (_accepts_columns, dispatch.py:226), while rs/php/ts
resolve column precedence in dispatch and leave render at 4 params.
Structurally divergent, behaviorally identical — which is precisely
what these fixtures verify. Every ordering case above passes on py
with the same expected sequence as the 4-param runtimes, so the
divergence is confined to the call shape.
Raw rendered bytes are NOT byte-comparable across runtimes and never
were: rs renders tables through comfy-table (leading/trailing cell
padding) while py/ts/php use a tabwriter shape, and php's YAML emits
the sequence dash on its own line where py/ts/rs inline it. Only
column ORDER is contractual, so the harness compares re-parsed column
sequences rather than bytes. Styling parity is contracts/parity's
job, not this suite's.
